idiom_name: ASP.NET Core authentication schemes: IAuthenticationHandler + AuthenticationHandler<TOptions>
implementation_notes: ASP.NET Core owns the seam: each mechanism is a handler implementing IAuthenticationHandler (InitializeAsync, AuthenticateAsync, ChallengeAsync, ForbidAsync), registered as a named scheme with AddAuthentication().AddJwtBearer()/AddCertificate()/AddScheme<TOptions, THandler>(), and resolved per request by scheme name through IAuthenticationService. Callers depend on HttpContext.User - a ClaimsPrincipal - so the mechanism stays configuration. Deriving from AuthenticationHandler<TOptions> replaces the classic abstract authenticator; a hand-written hierarchy is only justified outside ASP.NET Core or when the per-request handler instance model does not fit.
pitfalls: Returning NoResult for a present-but-invalid credential lets a later scheme authenticate the request; distinguish NoResult (not mine) from Fail (rejected).
Handlers are created per request, so caches (JWKS, trusted certificates) must be thread-safe and shared, not instance fields.
Scheme order and the default scheme decide fallbacks; an unintended default silently changes which mechanism runs.
Reading raw headers without going through the challenge flow means clients never receive WWW-Authenticate.
